title: A Review on Artificial Intelligence in Education
extended_summary:
This paper reviews the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in education and discusses how AI is changing teaching, learning, assessment, and school operations. The authors frame AI as a broad set of technologies that can support personalized instruction, automate routine teacher tasks, improve evaluation, and enable smarter educational environments.

Rather than testing one intervention, the paper synthesizes prior literature on several AI-enabled approaches, including adaptive learning systems, automated scoring and feedback, virtual classrooms, smart campus infrastructure, and intelligent tutoring robots. The review highlights examples such as ALEKS, BYJU’S, Duolingo, automated essay and speech scoring tools, and AI-supported classroom and campus management systems. These examples span school and higher-education contexts, with some emphasis on K-12 and especially adaptive education and tutoring applications.

The main conclusion is that AI has strong potential to improve personalized learning, teacher efficiency, educational equity, and campus management, but its adoption also raises concerns about fairness, ethics, data privacy, teacher readiness, and student self-regulation. The paper argues that successful AI integration in education requires coordinated effort from developers, teachers, students, and institutions, along with attention to contextual differences across countries and schools.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a narrative review, not a primary empirical study or meta-analysis conducted with full systematic methods in the paper itself. It synthesizes prior literature and cites individual studies, but the evidence base is heterogeneous and often descriptive, so methodological credibility is limited to review-level summarization.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests broad positive impacts for AI in education, but most claims are qualitative or based on scattered cited studies without pooled effect sizes. The likely impact is modest and context-dependent rather than clearly demonstrated at a medium or large level for K-12 science.

interventions.use_case: review of AI-enabled adaptive learning systems that personalize learning paths, pacing, and content using student data and analytics
review of AI systems for automated scoring, essay correction, homework grading, and test-paper feedback
review of intelligent tutoring robots and educational robots used for instruction, support, and interaction in school settings
review of AI-supported instructional platforms and digital teaching systems used to assist classroom learning and teaching

finding.finding_summary: The review cites a study of ALEKS showing a statistically significant positive impact on middle school students’ end-of-year mathematics scores. It also notes a meta-analysis finding ALEKS was about as effective as traditional classroom teaching overall, with better results when used for shorter periods rather than longer periods; no pooled effect size is reported in the paper text provided.
finding.measure: End-of-year mathematics scores; learning outcomes in ALEKS meta-analysis

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that AI-supported English learning platforms and speech recognition tools improved learners’ English performance and autonomous learning. For example, a college English teaching platform using AI was associated with higher average student scores than non-users, though the paper does not provide the sample size or effect size.
finding.measure: Average English scores; autonomous learning ability; pronunciation correction performance

finding.finding_summary: The review describes speech recognition and semantic analysis tools as supporting one-to-one oral practice and correcting pronunciation in English teaching. It also notes automated spoken-English assessment tools (e.g., SpeechRater) and reports improved oral-practice support, but no study-level effect sizes are given.
finding.measure: Oral practice, pronunciation correction, spoken English assessment

finding.finding_summary: Several cited studies suggest AI tools improved learners’ self-regulation, autonomy, and engagement. For instance, Duolingo was reported to increase autonomous learning behaviors such as self-regulation of study time and strategy adjustment, and the BYJU’S app was described as interactive and comfortable to use; no quantitative effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Autonomous learning/self-regulation; learner perceptions of interactivity and comfort

finding.finding_summary: A major theme of the review is that AI reduces teacher workload by automating routine tasks such as homework marking, test-paper scoring, question generation, attendance, and assessment. The article describes these effects qualitatively as improving efficiency and reducing teacher fatigue, but it does not report a pooled effect size or experimental estimate.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading time, assessment efficiency, attendance processing efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI-based smart campus systems improve administrative efficiency, safety, and resource allocation through face recognition, data monitoring, and automated access control. These claims are presented as descriptive benefits from prior studies rather than as a single evaluated effect, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Campus management efficiency, safety monitoring, resource allocation
